concepts.label: Malnutrition
concepts.definition: Any deficiency, excess or imbalance in the intake of energy or nutrients — a term that covers undernutrition and overweight together, not undernutrition alone.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given a patient with obesity, explain why the WHO definition classes them as malnourished.
concepts.pitfalls: Reading malnutrition as a synonym for undernutrition. The WHO definition covers excess and imbalance too, which is why the two can coexist in one country and one household.
originalWording: Malnutrition
evidenceGaps: The double burden of malnutrition, assessment of nutritional status, and the causes of each form are taught here and are not claim-backed.

concepts.label: Undernutrition
concepts.definition: The deficiency side of malnutrition, measured three ways: wasting is low weight-for-height, stunting is low height-for-age, and underweight is low weight-for-age.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given a child's anthropometry, say whether the problem is recent or long-standing.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating the three indices as interchangeable. Wasting is recent and acute; stunting is chronic and largely irreversible after early childhood.
originalWording: Undernutrition
evidenceGaps: Severe acute malnutrition, mid-upper arm circumference, oedematous malnutrition and refeeding syndrome are taught here and none are claim-backed. The corpus holds no candidate for stunting at all.

concepts.label: Micronutrient deficiency
concepts.definition: Inadequate intake or absorption of the vitamins and minerals the body needs in small amounts — of which iron deficiency, causing anaemia, is the most widespread.
concepts.explicitObjective: Name the groups most vulnerable to anaemia and say why each is at risk.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming a normal diet excludes micronutrient deficiency. Requirements rise in growth, menstruation and pregnancy, which is why the vulnerable groups are defined by physiological state rather than by poverty alone.
originalWording: Micronutrient deficiency
evidenceGaps: Vitamin A, iodine, zinc and vitamin D deficiency are each taught here and none are claim-backed. Only iron deficiency is covered by evidence in this batch.

concepts.label: Normal ageing
concepts.definition: The accumulation of molecular and cellular damage over time, which is neither linear nor consistent and tracks a person's age in years only loosely.
concepts.explicitObjective: Explain why chronological age is a poor guide to a patient's physiological reserve.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating age in years as a proxy for function. The cited evidence is that the association is loose, which is the whole argument for assessing the patient rather than the birth date.
originalWording: Normal ageing
evidenceGaps: Organ-specific age-related change, healthy ageing as a WHO construct, and the distinction between normal ageing and disease are taught here and none are claim-backed. No WHO page carrying a one-sentence definition of healthy ageing was found in this pass.

concepts.label: Preventive care
concepts.definition: Acting before disease, or before its consequences: primary prevention removes risk in the healthy, tertiary prevention limits the damage of established disease, and immunisation is the clearest instance of the first.
concepts.explicitObjective: Place a given intervention at the right level of prevention and say what it is acting on.
concepts.pitfalls: Reading prevention as advice. Immunisation, screening and environmental change are all prevention, and none of them is a conversation.
originalWording: Preventive care
evidenceGaps: Secondary prevention has no claim here. The only freely readable definition found is written around cardiovascular disease and does not generalise, so the level is named in the article and left unevidenced rather than cited to a source that means something narrower. The immunisation schedule, vaccine types and the threshold for herd immunity are also taught here and are not claim-backed.

concepts.label: Disability

concepts.pitfalls: Locating disability in the body alone. Both cited definitions place it partly outside the person: one in participation, the other explicitly in environmental factors.
originalWording: Disability
evidenceGaps: The two cited definitions do not say the same thing: the ICF triad is structural, WHO's current fact sheet is interactional, and the fact sheet no longer carries the triad. Both are recorded rather than reconciled. The ICF's body-function and environmental-factor components are not claim-backed.

concepts.label: Activities of daily living
concepts.definition: The basic skills needed to care for oneself, and the more complex instrumental activities needed to live independently in a community.
concepts.explicitObjective: Sort a list of tasks into basic and instrumental, and say what each loss would mean for where a person can live.
concepts.pitfalls: Assessing only the basic activities. Instrumental losses appear first and decide independence long before washing and dressing do.
originalWording: Activities of daily living
evidenceGaps: The named assessment scales, and the relationship between ADL loss and care needs, are taught here and are not claim-backed.

concepts.label: Health literacy
concepts.definition: The personal knowledge and competencies that accumulate through daily activities, social interactions and across generations — accumulated rather than taught, which is why a leaflet does not create it.
concepts.explicitObjective: Explain why the same explanation succeeds with one patient and fails with another.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating health literacy as a property of the patient to be worked around. The WHO definition also makes it a function of how services are organised.
originalWording: Health literacy
evidenceGaps: Communication techniques, interpreter use, accessible formats, and the organisational half of the WHO definition are taught here and none are claim-backed.

concepts.label: Reasonable adjustments
concepts.definition: Necessary and appropriate modifications that do not impose a disproportionate burden, made so that a person with a disability can exercise their rights on an equal basis with others.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given a barrier, propose an adjustment and say what would make it unreasonable.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating adjustments as goodwill. The cited definition frames them as what is required for equal exercise of rights, with proportionality as the limit.
originalWording: Reasonable adjustments
evidenceGaps: What counts as disproportionate, examples of adjustments in a clinical setting, and Egyptian legal obligations are all taught here and none are claim-backed.

concepts.label: Informal caregiver
concepts.definition: Someone, usually a family member, providing typically unpaid care to a person they have a personal relationship with — and who carries a measurable strain of their own.
concepts.explicitObjective: Say why the caregiver is also a patient in the consultation.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating the caregiver as a resource rather than a person. The strain is documented, and a caregiver who becomes unwell removes the care as well.
originalWording: Informal caregiver
evidenceGaps: Caregiver assessment, respite, and community support services are taught here and none are claim-backed. The phrase "caregiver burden" is deliberately not used: no freely readable authoritative source defining it was found, and the cited sources say caregiver stress.

concepts.label: Occupational health
concepts.definition: The field concerned with how work affects health — assessing workplace risks and preventing the diseases that arise from exposure to them.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given a disease and an occupation, say what would have to be true for it to count as occupational.
concepts.pitfalls: Calling a disease occupational because a worker has it. The definition requires a causal relationship with the working environment and a frequency above that of the rest of the population.
originalWording: Occupational health
evidenceGaps: Named occupational exposures and their diseases, workplace risk assessment, surveillance, and fitness for work are all taught here and none are claim-backed. The WHO occupational health topic page carries a definition of the field but displays no date, so it is not cited and the field is described from what its services do instead.

concepts.label: Lifestyle risk factors
concepts.definition: The four behaviours that drive most chronic disease — diet, physical activity, tobacco and alcohol — each modifiable, and each acting over decades rather than days.
concepts.explicitObjective: Name the four behavioural risk factors and say which chronic diseases they converge on.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating lifestyle as a matter of individual choice alone. Diet and activity are shaped by what is available and affordable, which is why these are addressed as population problems as well as personal ones.
originalWording: Lifestyle risk factors
evidenceGaps: Recommended intakes and activity levels, alcohol thresholds, the mechanisms by which each factor causes disease, and clustering of risk factors are all taught here and none are claim-backed. The WHO physical activity recommendation is stated on its fact sheet as a fragment following a heading rather than a complete sentence, so the amount is not quoted as a claim.

concepts.label: Risk assessment
concepts.definition: Estimating a person's probability of a future event from all their risk factors together, so that preventive action is matched to how likely the event actually is.
concepts.explicitObjective: Explain why two patients with the same blood pressure may warrant different action.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating each risk factor separately. The decision rests on total risk, so a modest abnormality in someone with several factors can matter more than a marked one in someone with none.
originalWording: Risk assessment
evidenceGaps: Risk charts and their inputs, the thresholds at which treatment is offered, ten-year against lifetime risk, and the difference between relative and absolute risk are all taught here and none are claim-backed. The total-risk principle is cited to a 2007 WHO guideline whose charts have since been superseded.

concepts.label: Family history
concepts.definition: Information about the patient's relatives covering heritable illness, current family health, psychosocial disorders and relationships — a risk assessment tool that costs nothing but time.
concepts.explicitObjective: Say what a family history tells you that a genetic test does not.
concepts.pitfalls: Reducing it to a list of diseases in relatives. The cited definition includes the family's current health, psychosocial disorders and relationships, which is what makes it useful when no genetic condition is present.
originalWording: Family history
evidenceGaps: Pedigree drawing and notation, the number of generations to record, patterns of inheritance, and which findings should prompt referral are all taught here and none are claim-backed. The cited source is a 1990 textbook edition
it is used for what a family history is and for nothing where practice has moved.

concepts.label: School health
concepts.definition: The school treated as a setting for health rather than only for teaching — where habits form, where a large population is reachable, and where health and education outcomes depend on each other.
concepts.explicitObjective: Say why a school is an efficient setting for preventive work.
concepts.pitfalls: Reading school health as screening children on school premises. The setting approach is about the environment, curriculum and services together, not a venue for clinics.
originalWording: School health
evidenceGaps: WHO's definition of a health-promoting school — "a school constantly strengthening its capacity as a healthy setting for living, learning and working" — sits on an initiative page that displays no date at all, so it is not cited and the concept is described from the two dated sources instead. The eight global standards, school health services, and the content of school health curricula are all taught here and none are claim-backed.

concepts.label: Plasma membrane
concepts.definition: The lipid bilayer enclosing every cell, which separates the cytosol from the extracellular fluid and controls what crosses between them.
concepts.explicitObjective: State what the plasma membrane separates and name the two properties — a hydrophobic core and embedded transport proteins — that make it selectively permeable.
concepts.pitfalls: Describing the membrane as a passive barrier. Its selectivity comes from the proteins embedded in it, so a substance that cannot cross the lipid core may still enter freely through a channel.
originalWording: Cell membrane structure and the fluid mosaic model
uncertainty: Local sources teach the fluid mosaic model at varying depth
the level expected in a first-year Egyptian examination is not yet established from the processed corpus.
evidenceGaps: The definition and objective are backed by claims with independent citations. The wider material in the linked article — membrane fluidity and drug transport — is not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Selective permeability
concepts.definition: The property of a biological membrane that allows some substances to cross while restricting others, determined jointly by the lipid core and the transport proteins present.
concepts.explicitObjective: Predict whether a given solute crosses a membrane by passive diffusion or requires a transport protein, from its size, charge and lipid solubility.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming small size alone predicts passage. A small ion such as Na⁺ is charged and cannot cross the lipid core unaided, while a much larger steroid dissolves through it readily.
originalWording: Membrane permeability and transport across the cell membrane
evidenceGaps: The core statement is claim-backed
the applied material in the linked article is not yet.

concepts.label: Cytoskeleton
concepts.definition: The protein filament network that gives a cell its shape, anchors its organelles, and provides the tracks along which intracellular transport and cell movement occur.
concepts.explicitObjective: Name the three filament classes — microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules — and state the distinct role each plays in shape, strength or transport.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating the cytoskeleton as a static scaffold. Microfilaments and microtubules are continuously assembled and disassembled, which is exactly what allows cell division and migration.
originalWording: Cytoskeleton: microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules
uncertainty: Only three processed sources teach this node, all from one university. Local emphasis elsewhere is unverified.
evidenceGaps: The core statement is claim-backed
the applied material in the linked article is not yet.

concepts.label: Cell nucleus
concepts.definition: The membrane-bound organelle that holds the cell's chromosomal DNA and is the site of DNA replication and transcription.
concepts.explicitObjective: State what the nuclear envelope separates, and explain why separating transcription from translation allows a eukaryotic cell to process its messenger RNA before it is read.
concepts.pitfalls: Calling the nucleus the site of protein synthesis. Transcription happens in the nucleus; translation happens on ribosomes in the cytoplasm, and the nuclear envelope is what keeps the two apart.
originalWording: Nucleus: nuclear envelope, chromatin and nucleolus
uncertainty: One of the three supporting sources is in a review-required state and cannot be relied on as evidence.
evidenceGaps: The core statement is claim-backed
the applied material in the linked article is not yet.

concepts.label: Mitochondrion
concepts.definition: The double-membraned organelle that carries out oxidative phosphorylation, generating most of a cell's ATP, and which holds its own small circular genome.
concepts.explicitObjective: State where in the mitochondrion the electron transport chain sits, and explain why a cell with high energy demand carries more mitochondria than one without.
concepts.pitfalls: Saying the mitochondrion "makes energy". It transfers energy already held in reduced carriers into ATP; it does not create it, and the distinction is what oxidative phosphorylation actually describes.
originalWording: Mitochondria: structure, cristae and the site of ATP production
uncertainty: Maternal inheritance of the mitochondrial genome is taught in some local sources and not others
whether it belongs to this concept or to a genetics concept is unresolved.
evidenceGaps: The core statement is claim-backed
the applied material in the linked article is not yet.

concepts.label: Cell cycle
concepts.definition: The ordered sequence a cell passes through from its creation at the end of one division until it divides again, comprising interphase and mitosis.
concepts.explicitObjective: Name the phases in order and state what the cell is doing in each, and say which checkpoint a given failure would be caught at.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating interphase as a resting stage. It is where the cell grows and replicates its entire genome, and it occupies most of the cycle.
originalWording: Cell cycle: interphase, mitosis and cytokinesis
uncertainty: Checkpoint detail varies between the Alexandria histology book and the pathology book
which depth a first-year examination expects is not established.
evidenceGaps: The checkpoint machinery and its cancer relevance are taught in the linked article but are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Cell-surface receptor
concepts.definition: A membrane protein that binds an extracellular signal molecule and, on binding, generates intracellular signals that change how the cell behaves.
concepts.explicitObjective: Explain why a signal that cannot cross the membrane can still change a cell's behaviour, and name the step that converts binding into an intracellular event.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming the receptor carries the signal molecule into the cell. It does not: binding changes the receptor, and the receptor generates a separate internal signal.
originalWording: Receptors and signal transduction across the cell membrane
evidenceGaps: Receptor families and their downstream pathways are taught in the linked article but are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Second messenger
concepts.definition: A small intracellular molecule generated in response to receptor activation, which carries and amplifies the signal inside the cell.
concepts.explicitObjective: State why the extracellular signal is called the first messenger and the intracellular one the second, and explain how this arrangement amplifies a small signal.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating amplification as a detail. One bound receptor can generate many second-messenger molecules, which is why a few hormone molecules can change a whole cell's behaviour.
originalWording: Second messengers in endocrine signalling
uncertainty: The Beni Suef endocrine book teaches second messengers in a hormone-specific way
whether the foundation course expects the general principle or the hormone examples is unresolved.
evidenceGaps: The named messengers — cyclic AMP, calcium, IP3 — are taught in the linked article but are not yet individually claim-backed.

concepts.label: Apoptosis
concepts.definition: Programmed cell death: a controlled, energy-dependent dismantling of a cell by its own machinery, leaving the surrounding tissue undisturbed.
concepts.explicitObjective: Distinguish apoptosis from necrosis by its trigger, its energy requirement and whether it provokes inflammation, and name the protease family that carries it out.
concepts.pitfalls: Equating cell death with damage. Apoptosis is a normal and necessary process, and failure of it is as pathological as excess of it.
originalWording: Apoptosis and necrosis: mechanisms of cell death
evidenceGaps: The intrinsic and extrinsic pathways, and the apoptosis–necrosis comparison, are taught in the linked article but only the definition and the caspase machinery are claim-backed.

concepts.label: Mendelian inheritance
concepts.definition: The transmission of a trait determined by a single gene, following the dominant and recessive patterns Mendel described.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given a pedigree, say which Mendelian pattern it fits, and state the recurrence risk that pattern predicts for the next child.
concepts.pitfalls: Reading an unaffected parent as a non-carrier. In a recessive condition both parents are usually unaffected carriers, and the risk to each pregnancy is one in four.
originalWording: Mendelian inheritance patterns
uncertainty: X-linked and codominant patterns are taught alongside the autosomal ones in the Alexandria book
whether the foundation examination expects all four is not established.
evidenceGaps: X-linked dominant and recessive patterns, and recurrence-risk arithmetic, are taught in the linked article but are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Chromosomal disorder
concepts.definition: A condition caused by a change in the number or structure of chromosomes rather than by a variant within a single gene.
concepts.explicitObjective: Distinguish a numerical from a structural chromosomal abnormality, and state why aneuploidy usually affects many body systems at once.
concepts.pitfalls: Expecting a single-gene inheritance pattern. Most aneuploidies arise from a new non-disjunction event and do not recur in a Mendelian pattern.
originalWording: Chromosomal disorders
evidenceGaps: Non-disjunction, structural rearrangements and the named trisomies are taught in the linked article
only the definition of aneuploidy is claim-backed.

concepts.label: Mitochondrial inheritance
concepts.definition: Transmission of variants in the mitochondrial genome, which passes from mother to all her children and from father to none.
concepts.explicitObjective: Recognise the pattern in a pedigree and explain why it follows from where the embryo gets its mitochondria.
concepts.pitfalls: Applying it to a father. An affected man transmits the variant to none of his children, which is the feature that separates this pattern from every autosomal one.
originalWording: Mitochondrial inheritance
evidenceGaps: Heteroplasmy and the threshold effect are taught in the linked article but are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Reversible cell injury
concepts.definition: Cell damage that stops short of the point of no return, so that the cell recovers fully once the stress is removed.
concepts.explicitObjective: State what distinguishes reversible from irreversible injury, and name the two changes seen earliest under the microscope.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating swelling as irreversible. Cellular swelling and fatty change both resolve completely if the stress is relieved in time.

the material is inferred from the adaptation and necrosis sources in the same books.
evidenceGaps: The morphological features of reversible injury are taught in the linked article but are not yet claim-backed. This concept currently borrows the adaptation claim and needs one of its own.

concepts.label: Necrosis
concepts.definition: Uncontrolled cell death following overwhelming injury, in which the cell swells and ruptures and its contents provoke inflammation.
concepts.explicitObjective: Distinguish necrosis from apoptosis on control, energy requirement, membrane integrity and inflammation, and name the common morphological patterns.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating all cell death as damage. Necrosis is uncontrolled and inflames; apoptosis is controlled and does not.
originalWording: Necrosis: types and morphology
evidenceGaps: The named necrosis patterns — coagulative, liquefactive, caseous, fat and fibrinoid — are taught in the linked article but are not yet individually claim-backed.

concepts.label: Cellular adaptation
concepts.definition: A reversible change in a cell’s size, number or type that keeps it within the limits of homeostasis under a new demand.
concepts.explicitObjective: Name the four adaptations and give a physiological and a pathological example of each.
concepts.pitfalls: Reading adaptation as disease. It is a successful response; it becomes pathological only when the stimulus persists beyond what the cell can accommodate.
originalWording: Cellular adaptations: hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy and metaplasia
evidenceGaps: Hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, metaplasia and dysplasia are each taught in the linked article
only the general definition of adaptation is claim-backed.

concepts.label: Acute inflammation
concepts.definition: The immediate, non-specific vascular and cellular response to injury, delivering plasma proteins and neutrophils to the affected tissue.
concepts.explicitObjective: Name the five cardinal signs and explain each from the underlying vascular or cellular change.
concepts.pitfalls: Learning the five signs as a list. Each follows from a specific change — vasodilatation, increased permeability, mediator action — and examinations ask for the mechanism, not the name.
originalWording: Acute inflammation
evidenceGaps: The vascular and cellular phases, the named mediators and the outcomes of acute inflammation are taught in the linked article
only the definition and the cardinal signs are claim-backed.

concepts.label: Chronic inflammation
concepts.definition: Inflammation persisting for months to years, in which tissue destruction and attempted repair proceed at the same time.
concepts.explicitObjective: State what distinguishes chronic from acute inflammation in duration, cell population and outcome, and say when granuloma formation occurs.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming chronic inflammation always follows acute. It can begin as chronic from the outset, as in a persistent intracellular infection or an autoimmune process.
originalWording: Chronic inflammation
uncertainty: The only local source is an MTI file the corpus marks review-required, so Egyptian curriculum emphasis for this node is weakly evidenced.
evidenceGaps: The cell populations, granuloma formation and the named chronic inflammatory diseases are taught in the linked article
only the definition is claim-backed.

concepts.label: Wound healing
concepts.definition: The ordered replacement of damaged tissue, passing through haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation and remodelling.
concepts.explicitObjective: Name the phases in order and state what is happening in each, and say why a wound regains strength long after it has closed.
concepts.pitfalls: Equating closure with healing. A wound that has closed is still remodelling and has not yet reached its final strength.
originalWording: Wound healing
evidenceGaps: Haemostasis, the inflammatory and remodelling phases, healing by first and second intention, and the factors that impair healing are taught in the linked article
only the proliferative phase is claim-backed.

concepts.label: Carcinogenesis
concepts.definition: The stepwise accumulation of genetic changes by which a normal cell acquires uncontrolled growth and the capacity to spread.
concepts.explicitObjective: Explain why cancer requires several changes rather than one, and name the two classes of gene whose alteration drives the process.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating cancer as a single mutation. It is a multi-step accumulation, which is why incidence rises so steeply with age.
originalWording: Carcinogenesis
evidenceGaps: Oncogenes, tumour suppressor genes, the multi-hit model and the named chemical, physical and viral carcinogens are taught in the linked article
only the definition of cancer is claim-backed. Egyptian carcinogen exposures are unaddressed and need local sourcing.

concepts.label: Tumour biology
concepts.definition: The properties that distinguish benign from malignant neoplasms, including growth pattern, invasion and the capacity to metastasise.
concepts.explicitObjective: Distinguish a benign from a malignant tumour on the features that actually matter, and explain why metastasis is the decisive one.

uncertainty: Only one processed local source teaches this node, so Egyptian curriculum emphasis is weakly evidenced.
evidenceGaps: The benign–malignant comparison, the routes of spread and tumour nomenclature are taught in the linked article

concepts.label: Grading and staging
concepts.definition: Two separate descriptions of a cancer: grade is how abnormal the cells look, stage is how far the disease has spread.
concepts.explicitObjective: State what grade and stage each measure, and explain why stage generally predicts outcome more strongly than grade.
concepts.pitfalls: Using the two words interchangeably. Grade is a microscopic appearance, stage is an anatomical extent, and a tumour can be high-grade but early-stage.
originalWording: Grading and staging of tumours
evidenceGaps: The TNM system and the numbered stages are taught in the linked article but are not yet claim-backed at the level of individual categories.

concepts.label: Pharmacokinetics
concepts.definition: The study of what the body does to a drug, over the whole period of exposure, through absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given a route of administration, predict which of the four processes most limits how much drug reaches the site of action.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating the four processes as sequential stages. They run concurrently from the moment of administration.
originalWording: Pharmacokinetics
evidenceGaps: First-pass metabolism, bioavailability, half-life, volume of distribution and clearance are each taught in the linked article
only the definition and the ADME list are claim-backed.

concepts.label: Pharmacodynamics
concepts.definition: The study of what a drug does to the body — its molecular, biochemical and physiological effects.
concepts.explicitObjective: State the difference between pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics in one sentence, and say which one a change in receptor number affects.

concepts.label: Dose–response relationship
concepts.definition: The relationship between the amount of drug given and the size of the effect produced, and the window between the least effective and the toxic dose.
concepts.explicitObjective: Read potency and efficacy off a dose–response curve, and say which of the two a competitive antagonist changes.
concepts.pitfalls: Reading a more potent drug as a better one. Potency is where the curve sits on the dose axis; efficacy is how high it reaches, and efficacy is what usually matters clinically.
originalWording: Dose-response relationships
evidenceGaps: Potency, efficacy, and the shapes produced by competitive and non-competitive antagonism are taught in the linked article
only the therapeutic window is claim-backed.

concepts.label: Therapeutic index
concepts.definition: A quantitative measure of a drug’s relative safety, comparing the dose that produces the wanted effect with the dose that produces toxicity.
concepts.explicitObjective: Say what a narrow therapeutic index implies for monitoring, and name what else must be considered before calling a drug safe.
concepts.pitfalls: Reading a high index as safe in every patient. The index is a population measure and says nothing about an individual whose handling of the drug is altered.
originalWording: Therapeutic index
uncertainty: Only one processed local source teaches this node, so Egyptian curriculum emphasis is weakly evidenced.
evidenceGaps: Which drugs are conventionally described as narrow-index, and the monitoring each requires, are not stated here and would each need their own evidence.

concepts.label: Adverse drug reaction
concepts.definition: A noxious and unintended response to a drug occurring at doses normally used for prophylaxis, diagnosis or therapy.
concepts.explicitObjective: Distinguish a dose-related reaction from an idiosyncratic one, and say which is predictable from the drug’s known action.

concepts.label: Bacteria
concepts.definition: Single-celled organisms without a nucleus, which can live independently and whose cell wall determines how they stain, what they resist, and which antibiotics reach them.

originalWording: Bacteria
evidenceGaps: Bacterial shape, growth requirements, spore formation and the named genera taught in this module are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Viruses
concepts.definition: Obligate intracellular parasites carrying either an RNA or a DNA genome inside a protein coat, which cannot reproduce without commandeering a host cell's machinery.
concepts.explicitObjective: Explain why an antibiotic cannot treat a viral infection, in terms of what a virus lacks.
concepts.pitfalls: Calling a virus a very small bacterium. It has no metabolism of its own, which is precisely why antibacterial drug targets do not exist in it.
originalWording: Viruses
evidenceGaps: The replication cycle, envelope structure and the named families taught in this module are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Parasites

concepts.label: Transmission

concepts.label: Colonization
concepts.definition: An organism present on a non-sterile body surface without causing disease — distinct from infection, which is an organism in a normally sterile site, or an organism that does not belong to the flora of that surface.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given a positive culture, decide whether it represents colonisation or infection, and say what in the clinical picture decides it.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating a positive culture as an indication to prescribe. A colonising organism is a normal finding at many sites, and treating it selects for resistance without helping the patient.
originalWording: Colonization
uncertainty: The local corpus holds a single record for this node, so curriculum emphasis is inferred rather than measured.
evidenceGaps: Normal flora by site, and the clinical criteria that distinguish contamination from colonisation from infection, are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Specimen collection
concepts.definition: Taking a sample that genuinely represents the disease process, in sufficient quantity, and before antimicrobials are given — because everything the laboratory can report is limited by what arrives in the container.

concepts.pitfalls: Sending a specimen through a contaminated surface without either disinfecting it or bypassing it. The result then describes the surface flora rather than the infection.
originalWording: Specimen collection
evidenceGaps: Container choice, transport media, transport time limits and site-specific technique are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Culture
concepts.definition: Growing an organism from a specimen on artificial media or in a living host, so that it can be identified and tested — using non-selective media that permit many organisms, or selective media that suppress all but the ones sought.
concepts.explicitObjective: Choose between a selective and a non-selective medium for a given specimen, and justify the choice from what else lives at that site.
concepts.pitfalls: Expecting culture to recover every organism. Some pathogens do not grow on routine media at all, so a negative culture excludes far less than it appears to.
originalWording: Culture
evidenceGaps: Named media, colony morphology, incubation conditions and the interpretation of a susceptibility report are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Molecular tests
concepts.definition: Diagnosis by amplifying and detecting a pathogen's nucleic acid rather than growing the organism, which finds what culture cannot and reports in hours rather than days.

concepts.label: Sterilization

concepts.label: Ischaemia

concepts.label: Body fluid compartments
concepts.definition: The division of total body water into an intracellular and an extracellular volume, with the extracellular volume further split between interstitial fluid and plasma.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given a litre of fluid lost or gained, predict which compartment changes most and why.
concepts.pitfalls: Reading the compartments as separate tanks. Water moves freely between them along osmotic gradients, which is why a sodium problem is usually a water problem.
originalWording: Body fluid compartments
uncertainty: The cited figures are for an average 70 kg man. Total body water varies with age, sex and body composition, and that variation is not claim-backed here.
evidenceGaps: Osmolality, tonicity, the Starling forces governing movement between plasma and interstitium, and how the figures change with age and sex are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Hypovolaemia
concepts.definition: A low extracellular fluid volume, usually after losing sodium and water together, so that the compartment which fills the vessels is the one that shrinks.
concepts.explicitObjective: Explain why losing sodium and water together depletes the circulation more than losing water alone.
concepts.pitfalls: Equating hypovolaemia with dehydration. Losing water alone raises sodium and draws fluid out of cells; losing salt and water together empties the extracellular space directly.
originalWording: Hypovolaemia
uncertainty: The only plain one-sentence definition available is in a StatPearls chapter that has been archived. Its current replacement defines hypovolaemic shock instead. The definition is standard, but its source is no longer maintained.
evidenceGaps: Clinical assessment of volume status, the distinction from shock, and fluid replacement are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Hyponatraemia
concepts.definition: A serum sodium below the reference range, caused by an excess of body water relative to body sodium rather than by a shortage of sodium as such.
concepts.explicitObjective: Explain why hyponatraemia is usually a water problem, and what that implies for treating it.
concepts.pitfalls: Correcting hyponatraemia by giving sodium without asking about water. The excess water is usually the abnormality, and correcting too quickly causes harm of its own.
originalWording: Hyponatraemia
uncertainty: The cited source notes the 135 mEq/L threshold may vary slightly with the laboratory reference range, so the number is a convention rather than a constant.
evidenceGaps: Volume-status classification, symptom thresholds, correction rate limits and osmotic demyelination are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Hypernatraemia
concepts.definition: A serum sodium above the reference range, which in practice almost always means a water deficit rather than an excess of sodium.

uncertainty: That hypernatraemia usually reflects a water deficit rather than sodium excess is standard teaching and is stated here without its own citation.
evidenceGaps: Causes, the role of thirst and access to water, and correction rate limits are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Hypokalaemia
concepts.definition: A serum potassium below the lower limit of normal, graded by severity, and important chiefly for what it does to cardiac and neuromuscular excitability.
concepts.explicitObjective: Grade a given potassium value by severity, and say what you would look for on an ECG.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating a number without asking where the potassium went. Shift into cells and true depletion look identical on the result and need different treatment.
originalWording: Hypokalaemia
conflicts: Two authoritative sources disagree on the threshold. The dedicated StatPearls Hypokalemia chapter gives a lower limit of normal of 3.5 mmol/L
the StatPearls Electrolytes chapter defines hypokalaemia as under 3.6 mmol/L. This library follows the dedicated chapter and records the disagreement rather than hiding it.
evidenceGaps: ECG changes, causes, the interaction with magnesium, and replacement are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Metabolic acidosis
concepts.definition: A fall in serum bicarbonate, with the lungs compensating by lowering arterial pCO2 — the metabolic half of the acid-base pair.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given a blood gas, decide whether the primary problem is metabolic or respiratory.
concepts.pitfalls: Reading a compensating pCO2 as a second disorder. Compensation is the expected response to the primary problem, not an additional one.
originalWording: Metabolic acidosis
evidenceGaps: Named causes, the limits of expected compensation, and mixed disorders are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Respiratory acidosis
concepts.definition: Accumulation of carbon dioxide from failure of ventilation, which the kidney compensates for by retaining bicarbonate.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given a raised pCO2, say what the bicarbonate should be doing and over what timescale.
concepts.pitfalls: Expecting renal compensation immediately. It takes days, so an acute and a chronic respiratory acidosis show very different bicarbonate values for the same pCO2.
originalWording: Respiratory acidosis
uncertainty: The timescale of renal compensation is standard teaching and is stated here without its own citation.
evidenceGaps: Acute against chronic compensation, named causes of ventilatory failure, and the expected compensation formulae are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Anion gap
concepts.definition: The difference between the measured cations and measured anions in the metabolic panel, used to sort metabolic acidosis into two groups by what is producing the acid.
concepts.explicitObjective: Calculate an anion gap and say which group of causes a raised value points to.
concepts.pitfalls: Reading the gap without checking albumin. Albumin is a major unmeasured anion, so a low albumin lowers the gap and can hide a raised one.
originalWording: Anion gap
evidenceGaps: The correction for albumin, the named causes in each group, and the delta ratio are not yet claim-backed.

concepts.label: Drug distribution
concepts.definition: The movement of unchanged drug from the blood into the tissues, which is uneven because perfusion, tissue binding, pH and membrane permeability all differ from one tissue to the next.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given two tissues, say which will see more drug and why.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming a drug reaches all tissues equally. Distribution is uneven by default, and the unevenness is what makes some sites hard to treat.
originalWording: Drug distribution
uncertainty: The source plan lists local sources for this node, but they match on the word rather than the sense — the highest-ranked file is a research-methods book for "distribution" and a haematology book for "metabolism". No local course book was found teaching this in its pharmacokinetic sense, so no local citation is offered and the node is authored from independent sources alone.
evidenceGaps: Barriers such as the blood-brain barrier, redistribution, and the effect of displacement from protein binding are taught here and are not claim-backed.

concepts.label: Drug metabolism
concepts.definition: Chemical modification of a drug into metabolites, conventionally in two phases: direct modification of the molecule, then conjugation to a small polar molecule.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given a drug and its metabolite, say which phase produced it.
concepts.pitfalls: Assuming metabolism inactivates. It changes the molecule; the metabolite can be inactive, active, or more toxic than the parent.

No local course book was found teaching this in its pharmacokinetic sense, so no local citation is offered and the node is authored from independent sources alone.
evidenceGaps: Prodrugs, active and toxic metabolites, enzyme induction and inhibition, and extrahepatic metabolism are taught here and are not claim-backed.

concepts.label: Cytochrome P450
concepts.definition: The enzyme family that carries out most phase I drug metabolism, and therefore the site of most clinically important metabolic drug interactions.
concepts.explicitObjective: Explain why two drugs handled by the same CYP enzyme can interact.
concepts.pitfalls: Treating induction and inhibition as symmetrical. Inhibition is fast because it competes for the existing enzyme; induction is slow because it requires new enzyme to be made.
originalWording: Cytochrome P450
evidenceGaps: Named isoenzymes, inducers and inhibitors, and the timescale difference between induction and inhibition are taught here and are not claim-backed.

concepts.label: First-pass effect
concepts.definition: Metabolism of a drug before it reaches the systemic circulation, which lowers the concentration that arrives at the site of action.
concepts.explicitObjective: Explain why the oral and intravenous doses of the same drug can differ greatly.
concepts.pitfalls: Thinking of it as loss in the gut. The main site is the liver the drug passes through before reaching the systemic circulation.
originalWording: First-pass effect
evidenceGaps: Bioavailability as a number, the routes that bypass the first pass, and named high-extraction drugs are taught here and are not claim-backed.

concepts.label: Clearance
concepts.definition: The ratio of a drug's elimination rate to its plasma concentration — the parameter that determines the maintenance dose.
concepts.explicitObjective: Explain why clearance and not half-life determines the maintenance dose.
concepts.pitfalls: Reading clearance as an amount removed. It is a rate relative to concentration, which is why it stays constant while the amount removed falls.
originalWording: Clearance
evidenceGaps: The relationship between clearance, volume of distribution and half-life, and the maintenance-dose calculation, are taught here and are not claim-backed.

concepts.label: Half-life
concepts.definition: The time taken for the serum concentration of a drug to fall by half, which sets the dosing interval and the time to steady state.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given a half-life, say how long until steady state and how long until the drug has effectively gone.
concepts.pitfalls: Reading half-life as how long the drug works. It describes concentration decay, and duration of effect also depends on where the effective concentration sits.
originalWording: Half-life
evidenceGaps: The five-half-lives rule for steady state and washout, and the distinction between elimination and effect-site half-life, are taught here and are not claim-backed.

concepts.label: Pharmacokinetics in special populations
concepts.definition: How drug handling differs at the extremes of age, in organ impairment, and in pregnancy — almost always a change in kinetics rather than in the drug's action.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given an older patient with reduced renal function, say which pharmacokinetic step changed and what follows for the dose.
concepts.pitfalls: Adjusting the dose for age as a rule of thumb. What changed is a measurable kinetic step, usually renal elimination, and the adjustment follows from that rather than from the birth date.
originalWording: Pharmacokinetics in special populations
uncertainty: The local corpus holds no records at this node. Pregnancy is the weakest-sourced of the four populations: the one verified sentence is incidental to an article about distribution, and no dedicated freely readable source on pregnancy pharmacokinetics was located.
evidenceGaps: Named dose-adjustment rules, creatinine-clearance estimation, hepatic impairment, and paediatric weight-based dosing are all taught here and none are claim-backed.

concepts.label: Cysteine gives cystine, enzyme thiol groups, the sulfate of PAPS, thioethanolamine of coenzyme A, taurine and glutathione
concepts.definition: Cysteine is the non-essential sulfur amino acid, synthesised by the trans-sulfuration pathway in which cystathionine synthase condenses homocysteine with serine to give cystathionine, and cystathionase then splits cystathionine into homoserine and cysteine; both enzymes need pyridoxal phosphate. It is glucogenic, being converted to pyruvate. The department book gives it six derivatives, and every one of them is a different use of the same sulfur atom. Two molecules of cysteine are oxidised to cystine, joined by a disulfide bond. The thiol group is a component of the active site of many enzymes. Cysteine provides the sulfate group of phosphoadenosyl-phosphosulfate, PAPS or active sulfate, the sulfate donor for glycosaminoglycans, sulfolipids and detoxification. It makes thioethanolamine, a component of coenzyme A. It makes taurine, mainly in liver cells, which is conjugated with bile acids like glycine and excreted in bile as bile salts. And it is one of the three amino acids of glutathione, with glycine and glutamic acid.

concepts.label: Fumarate is where the urea cycle meets the citric acid cycle, and the aspartate–argininosuccinate shunt hands the carbon back
aliases: Link between urea cycle and citric acid cycle
Fate of the carbon skeleton of aspartate
concepts.arabicLabel: الفومارات كحلقة الوصل بين دورة اليوريا ودورة حمض الستريك
concepts.definition: Aspartate enters the cytosolic arm of the urea cycle and is joined to citrulline to form argininosuccinate. Argininosuccinase then cleaves that molecule in two: arginine keeps the nitrogen and goes on to yield urea, while the four carbons aspartate brought in leave as fumarate. Fumarate is an intermediate of the citric acid cycle, so it is the compound at which the two cycles meet. From there the citric acid cycle's own reactions carry the carbon round and back: fumarase hydrates fumarate to malate, malate dehydrogenase oxidises malate to oxaloacetate, and AST transaminates oxaloacetate to aspartate, which re-enters the urea cycle. The urea cycle therefore borrows a carbon skeleton and returns it, and malate sits one step past the junction rather than at it.
concepts.explicitObjective: Name fumarate as the compound linking the urea cycle to the citric acid cycle, and trace the carbon of aspartate out of the urea cycle and back into it.
concepts.pitfalls: Answering malate. Malate is what actually crosses back to rejoin the citric acid cycle, but it is made by fumarase after the link has been formed; the compound the urea cycle itself releases is fumarate. The other slip is choosing citrate by matching "citr-" to "citrulline", which is a spelling coincidence and not a chemical relationship.
moduleSubjectPaths: 103 BMS > Biochemistry > General protein Metabolism > Urea Cycle
originalWording: "Cleavage of argininosuccinate by argininosuccinate lyase produces fumarate and arginine."
"Aspartate + NH3 + CO2 + 3ATP → Urea + fumarate + 2ADP + 2 Pi +AMP + PPi"
uncertainty: The book never uses the phrase "aspartate–argininosuccinate shunt" and nowhere states in a sentence that the two cycles are linked. What it prints is the arc itself, drawn on the urea cycle figure: fumarate, fumarase, L-malate, malate dehydrogenase, oxaloacetate and AST, closing back onto aspartate. The link is therefore read off a figure rather than off prose, which is why support_mode is inferred_from_figure — and the question book asks for it directly, so it is examined even though the sentence is not printed.

concepts.label: Folate antagonists work at two different enzymes, and that is why one is an antibiotic and the other an anticancer drug
concepts.definition: The book names two folate antagonists and they act at different points. Sulfonamides are competitive inhibitors of the bacterial enzyme that incorporates PABA into folic acid, so bacteria cannot make folate and cannot multiply; they do not affect human DNA or RNA synthesis, because mammalian cells cannot synthesise folic acid at all and must take it in. Methotrexate is an anticancer drug and a competitive inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase, so folic acid is not activated to tetrahydrofolate, and DNA synthesis and cell division of malignant cells stop — the conversion of dUMP to dTMP needs methylene-THF. Treatment with methotrexate is itself a listed cause of folate deficiency.
concepts.explicitObjective: Name the two folate antagonists the book gives, state the enzyme each inhibits, and explain why one is selective for bacteria and the other is not.
concepts.pitfalls: Saying sulfonamides are selective because they only enter bacteria. The selectivity is metabolic, not a matter of uptake: human cells have no folate synthesis pathway to inhibit, so the enzyme sulfonamides block does not exist in them. Methotrexate blocks an enzyme humans do have, which is precisely why it causes folate deficiency.

concepts.label: Body protein is in a dynamic steady state, and it is burnt for energy only when carbohydrate and fat cannot spare it
aliases: Protein as a source of energy
concepts.arabicLabel: دوران البروتين والحالة الديناميكية لبروتينات الجسم
concepts.definition: Cellular proteins are continuously degraded and resynthesised, so a constant body protein content is a balance between two large opposing fluxes rather than a static store; about 75 per cent of the amino acids released are reutilised and the rest are rapidly degraded. Protein yields 4 kcal/g, nearly the same as carbohydrate and less than half that of fat, and the presence of carbohydrate and fat in the diet spares protein from oxidation, so amino acids are used for energy only when those fuels are inadequate.
concepts.explicitObjective: Explain why a steady body protein content is a steady state rather than a static one, and predict when amino acids will be oxidised for energy from the availability of carbohydrate and fat.
concepts.pitfalls: Reading nitrogen equilibrium as "nothing is happening to body protein", so that turnover is treated as something that stops after growth ends. It does not stop, which is why an adult still has a daily protein requirement and why any illness that raises catabolism produces negative nitrogen balance within days.

concepts.label: The purine ring is assembled from five sources, and only three of them — glutamine, aspartate and glycine — donate nitrogen
aliases: Sources of the atoms of the purine ring
Nitrogen donors of the purine ring
concepts.arabicLabel: مصادر ذرات حلقة البيورين في التخليق الابتدائي
concepts.definition: De novo synthesis builds the purine ring atom by atom onto a ribose phosphate. The hexose monophosphate pathway supplies ribose-5-phosphate, PRPP synthetase converts it to PRPP, and glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase then donates the amide nitrogen of glutamine to give 5-phosphoribosylamine — the step the book calls the key step of de novo purine nucleotide synthesis. The ring is completed to inosine monophosphate, and the book's figure names five sources for its nine atoms: the amide group of glutamine, aspartate, glycine, respiratory CO2 and N10-formyl-THF. Only the first three carry nitrogen. Glycine enters as an intact unit contributing carbon as well as nitrogen, and folate supplies two carbons — which is why folate antagonists such as methotrexate block purine and nucleic acid synthesis and so inhibit cell division.
concepts.explicitObjective: Name the five sources of the purine ring atoms, pick out the three that donate nitrogen, and distinguish the amide nitrogen of glutamine from the α-amino nitrogen of glutamate.
concepts.pitfalls: Answering glutamate instead of glutamine. Glutamate is the collector of amino acid nitrogen everywhere else in protein metabolism, so it is the name a student reaches for; but the donor here is the amide group of glutamine, and amide nitrogen and α-amino nitrogen are different chemistry. The second error is dropping glycine from the list because it is remembered as a carbon donor — it contributes an intact nitrogen-carbon-carbon unit and gives both.

concepts.label: Ammonia and aspartate donate the two nitrogen atoms of urea, three ATP pay for one turn, and N-acetylglutamate is what commits carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
aliases: Overall reaction of the urea cycle
ATP cost of the urea cycle
Rate limiting step of urea synthesis
concepts.arabicLabel: المعادلة الإجمالية لدورة اليوريا: مصدرا النيتروجين وتكلفة الطاقة والمنظِّم
concepts.definition: The book prints the whole cycle as a single equation — aspartate + NH3 + CO2 + 3 ATP → urea + fumarate + 2 ADP + 2 Pi + AMP + PPi — and every term in it is examined. The two nitrogen atoms of urea come from two different donors entering in two different compartments. The first is free ammonia, condensed with bicarbonate at the expense of 2 ATP by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the mitochondrial matrix. The second is the amino group of aspartate, joined to citrulline by argininosuccinate synthetase in the cytosol, which is why aspartate is the amino acid the cycle needs alongside CO2, NH3 and ATP. The price is three molecules of ATP but four high-energy phosphate bonds, because the third is hydrolysed to AMP and PPi rather than to ADP. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is the rate-limiting enzyme and is absolutely dependent on N-acetylglutamate, which is made from acetyl-CoA and glutamate in a reaction arginine activates — so a protein-rich meal supplies both the substrate and the regulator, and the rate of urea synthesis follows protein intake.
concepts.explicitObjective: Read the overall equation of the urea cycle back: name the two nitrogen donors and the compartment each enters in, state the cost as both molecules of ATP and high-energy bonds, and name the enzyme and the activator that set the rate.
concepts.pitfalls: Answering "glutamate" for the second nitrogen donor. Glutamate is the collector of nitrogen from every amino acid and is upstream of both donors, but it enters the cycle either as free ammonia after deamination or as aspartate after transamination, never as glutamate itself. The second slip is answering four ATP because four high-energy bonds are broken: the book's figure for molecules of ATP consumed is three.

Read strictly, one turn breaks four high-energy bonds while consuming three ATP molecules, and the book never reconciles the two sentences. concepts.label: Glutamate dehydrogenase does the deamination that matters; L-amino acid oxidase is a low-activity liver and kidney enzyme
concepts.definition: Two enzymes carry out oxidative deamination. L-amino acid oxidase is an FMN-containing flavoprotein of low activity that works only in liver and kidney, producing the α-keto acid, ammonia and hydrogen peroxide, which catalase then destroys. L-glutamate dehydrogenase is a mitochondrial NAD(P)+-dependent enzyme of high activity and wide distribution that converts glutamate to α-ketoglutarate; it is the essential component of transdeamination and, being reversible, also resynthesises glutamate from free ammonia and NAD(P)H.
concepts.explicitObjective: Contrast the two oxidative deaminating enzymes on cofactor, activity, distribution and importance, and explain why the low-activity one cannot account for most ammonia release.
concepts.pitfalls: Choosing L-amino acid oxidase as the main route because it acts on a wide range of amino acids while glutamate dehydrogenase acts on one. Breadth of substrate is not throughput: the oxidase is of low activity and confined to two organs, and it is the transaminases that give the dehydrogenase its breadth by funnelling every amino group onto glutamate.
moduleSubjectPaths: 103 BMS > Biochemistry > General protein Metabolism > Removal of Amino Acid Nitrogen
originalWording: "This enzyme is a flavoprotein containing FMN. It is of low activity. It works only in the liver and kidneys."

"It is a mitochondrial enzyme. This enzyme is NAD(P)+-dependent dehydrogenase that converts L-glutamate into α-Ketoglutarate. It is of high activity and widespread distribution in tissues. It is an essential component of transdeamination reaction"
uncertainty: The book does not quantify "low activity" for L-amino acid oxidase or say what fraction of ammonia release it accounts for, so the claim that the dehydrogenase route dominates is qualitative in this source.
evidenceGaps: Evidence must be attached before publication.

concepts.label: Alkaptonuria is deficiency of homogentisate oxidase: the urine is normal when passed and blackens as it stands, and the same quinones stain bone and cartilage
concepts.arabicLabel: البيلة السوداء ونقص إنزيم أكسيديز الهوموجنتيسات
concepts.definition: Alkaptonuria is caused by deficiency of homogentisate oxidase, the vitamin C and Fe²⁺ dependent enzyme that opens the ring of homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate on the catabolic branch of tyrosine. Homogentisate accumulates in the tissues and is excreted in the urine, where it undergoes auto-oxidation into quinones, which are deep brown. The child voids urine of normal colour and it soon darkens to black, because the oxidation happens in air rather than in the bladder. The same quinones give the tissues — particularly bone and cartilage — a brown colour, a condition called ochronosis, and the patient suffers arthritis.
concepts.explicitObjective: Identify alkaptonuria from a history of urine that is normal when passed and darkens on standing, name homogentisate oxidase as the deficient enzyme, and place the block relative to phenylketonuria and albinism on the same pathway.
concepts.pitfalls: Reaching for tyrosinase because the word "pigment" is in the stem: tyrosinase deficiency is albinism, which is too little pigment of a different kind, and the enzyme is on the synthetic branch rather than the catabolic one. The second is picking the enzyme one step too late — a block at the hydrolase after homogentisate oxidase lets no homogentisate accumulate and gives no black urine. The third is tyrosine aminotransferase, which is one step too early: a block there raises tyrosine and produces no homogentisate at all.
moduleSubjectPaths: 103 BMS > Biochemistry > Individual amino acid Metabolism > Aromatic Amino Acids (Phenylalanine and Tyrosine)
originalWording: "Alkaptonuria: Cause: deficiency of homogentisate oxidase."

"Homogentisate accumulates in tissues and is excreted in urine. It undergoes auto-oxidation into quinones (deep brown). Quinones give the tissues, particularly bone and cartilage, the brown color. This condition is called ochronosis. The patient suffers from arthritis (joint pains)."
"The child void urine of normal color, but soon it darkens to black."
uncertainty: The book says the quinones colour the tissues brown and separately that the patient suffers arthritis, without saying that the deposition is what causes the joint disease. The causal step is not printed and is not asserted here.
evidenceGaps: Evidence must be attached before publication.

concepts.label: The mental retardation of PKU comes from what phenylalanine keeps out of the brain, not from phenylalanine itself
aliases: Causes for neurological manifestation in PKU
Amino acid transport competition at the blood-brain barrier
concepts.arabicLabel: سبب المظاهر العصبية في بيلة الفينيل كيتون
arabicAliases: التخلف العقلي في بيلة الفينيل كيتون
concepts.definition: Two things happen at once. Raised phenylalanine and its metabolites interfere with the transport of tyrosine and tryptophan into the brain, so the brain is short of both. And because phenylalanine cannot be hydroxylated, tyrosine is low to begin with, which impairs synthesis of the neurotransmitters derived from it — DOPA and the catecholamines dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline. The book gives this as the explanation for why an untreated patient shows mental retardation, manifest by the age of one year.
concepts.explicitObjective: Explain the cause of the neurological manifestations of PKU in two steps, naming the amino acids kept out of the brain and the neurotransmitters that are consequently not made.
concepts.pitfalls: Saying phenylalanine is directly toxic to neurones. The book's mechanism is competition and deprivation: phenylalanine blocks tyrosine and tryptophan from entering the brain, and the missing tyrosine means missing neurotransmitters. Answering "high phenylalanine damages the brain" restates the finding instead of explaining it and earns nothing.
moduleSubjectPaths: 103 BMS > Biochemistry > Individual amino acid Metabolism > Aromatic Amino Acids (Phenylalanine and Tyrosine)
originalWording: [Biochemistry III, Case (1) b (second occurrence of the letter b), 1 mark] Causes for neurological manifestation:

"The elevated phenylalanine and its metabolites will interfere with the transport of tyrosine and tryptophan to the brain leading to their deficiency. Also decreased tyrosine leads to impaired neurotransmitters synthesis in the brain
and this may explain why untreated patient shows mental retardation that manifest by the age of one year."
uncertainty: The book itself hedges — "this may explain why untreated patient shows mental retardation" — so the mechanism is offered as an explanation rather than as an established one, and it is written here with the same hedge. What tryptophan deficiency contributes, as against tyrosine deficiency, is not separated in the source.
evidenceGaps: Supported by the department book only, and the book states the mechanism tentatively. Nothing here should be published as settled without a second source.

concepts.label: Tyrosine is non-essential and mixed: its catabolism ends in fumarate, which is glucogenic, and acetoacetate, which is ketogenic
concepts.arabicLabel: التيروسين حمض أميني مختلط غير أساسي
arabicAliases: حمض أميني مولد للجلوكوز ومولد للكيتونات
concepts.definition: Tyrosine is non-essential because phenylalanine hydroxylase makes it from phenylalanine, and it is a mixed amino acid because its catabolism ends in two different kinds of product. Tyrosine aminotransferase, a PLP enzyme, transaminates it with α-ketoglutarate to p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate; p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate hydroxylase, needing vitamin C and Cu²⁺, converts that to homogentisate and releases CO2; homogentisate oxidase, needing vitamin C and Fe²⁺, opens the ring to maleylacetoacetate; an isomerase and then a hydrolase split it into fumarate, which is glucogenic, and acetoacetate, which is ketogenic. The book's summary table lists tyrosine as mixed and non-essential, and phenylalanine as mixed and essential.
concepts.explicitObjective: Classify tyrosine as non-essential and mixed, name fumarate and acetoacetate as its two catabolic end products, and explain why phenylalanine's carbon enters the citric acid cycle as fumarate.
concepts.pitfalls: Calling tyrosine essential because a phenylketonuric child must be given it. The book's table lists it as non-essential, and the dietary requirement in PKU follows from the missing enzyme rather than from any property of the amino acid. The second slip is looking for a catabolic route of phenylalanine's own: there is none in this book, because phenylalanine is catabolised only after it has been converted to tyrosine.

concepts.label: PKU is treated by removing phenylalanine from the diet and putting tyrosine back, and it must start before the damage is done
concepts.definition: The book states that PKU is treatable by dietary means and that early diagnosis is what avoids the mental retardation. Treatment of classic PKU is dietary restriction of phenylalanine, using a phenylalanine-free milk formula, together with tyrosine supplementation — tyrosine has become an essential amino acid for this patient because they cannot make it. In the rare cases caused by BH4 deficiency rather than by PAH deficiency, the treatment is both dietary and supplementation of BH4.
concepts.explicitObjective: State the treatment of classic PKU and of the BH4-deficient variant, and explain why tyrosine has to be supplied rather than merely allowed.
concepts.pitfalls: Writing "a protein-free diet". Phenylalanine is restricted, not eliminated and not extended to all protein — it is an essential amino acid and a growing infant still needs some. Forgetting the tyrosine supplement is the other half-answer, and it is the half that explains why the treatment works.

concepts.label: Transamination is reversible and pyridoxal-phosphate dependent, and α-ketoglutarate is the amino-group acceptor in every one of them
concepts.definition: Transamination transfers an amino group from an α-amino acid to an α-keto acid, forming a new α-keto acid and a new α-amino acid, and requires pyridoxal phosphate as the intermediate carrier of the amino group. It takes up and releases no free ammonia. α-Ketoglutarate is the amino-group acceptor in all transamination reactions, so glutamate collects nitrogen from every amino acid, and because the reaction is reversible it serves both deamination and the biosynthesis of the non-essential amino acids from carbohydrate intermediates — pyruvate to alanine by ALT, oxaloacetate to aspartate by AST.
concepts.explicitObjective: Write a transamination reaction with its four participants and its cofactor, and explain how one reversible reaction serves both nitrogen disposal and non-essential amino acid synthesis.
concepts.pitfalls: Believing transamination runs only one way — that it converts an α-amino acid into an α-keto acid but not the reverse. Held that way, the body could not make a single non-essential amino acid by transamination, and every question about aminating a carbon skeleton becomes unanswerable.
moduleSubjectPaths: 103 BMS > Biochemistry > General protein Metabolism > Removal of Amino Acid Nitrogen
originalWording: "The reaction is reversible, so it is important in deamination and in the biosynthesis of the nonessential amino acids. It requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) as intermediate carrier of the amino group."

concepts.label: Ammonia travels as glutamine from brain and as alanine from muscle, and it injures the brain three ways when the liver cannot clear it
concepts.definition: Ammonia is produced continuously yet held below about 0.05 mg/dL in blood, because it is carried in non-toxic forms and disposed of. Glutamine synthetase condenses ammonia with glutamate to give glutamine, which is the major route of ammonia removal in the brain and is hydrolysed by glutaminase in liver and kidney; muscle instead transfers its amino acid nitrogen onto pyruvate by ALT and sends alanine to the liver in the glucose-alanine cycle. When clearance fails, the brain is injured three ways: α-ketoglutarate is pulled into glutamate, depleting a citric acid cycle intermediate and cutting ATP production; GABA becomes deficient and convulsions may follow; and glutamine accumulating in astrocytes causes osmotic brain oedema.
concepts.explicitObjective: Name the transport form of ammonia used by each organ, and give the three mechanisms by which hyperammonaemia damages the brain.
concepts.pitfalls: Answering "glutamine" for the muscle-to-liver carrier because glutamine is the better-known transport form. The book gives glutamine for the brain and alanine for muscle, and the two are asked about separately.

concepts.label: Negative nitrogen balance has three causes: too little protein in, too much protein lost, too much protein broken down
concepts.definition: Nitrogen forms about 16 per cent of protein, so the difference between nitrogen intake and nitrogen output measures the balance between protein anabolism and catabolism. Negative nitrogen balance exists when output exceeds intake, and the book gives three causes. Inadequate protein intake, in starvation, malnutrition, deficiency of an essential amino acid, and gastrointestinal disease. Loss of protein, in chronic haemorrhage, albuminuria, and lactation on an inadequate diet. Increased protein catabolism, in diabetes mellitus, Cushing's syndrome, hyperthyroidism, and infectious fevers.
concepts.explicitObjective: Give the three causes of negative nitrogen balance and place at least one clinical example under each.
concepts.pitfalls: Answering with examples instead of causes — "starvation, bleeding, fever" — which is a list of six things in no order rather than the three headings the book uses. The mark scheme follows the book's structure, and a student who gives two of the three headings has two marks whatever examples they add.

concepts.label: The water-soluble vitamins are coenzymes, and a matching question tests which reaction each one runs
aliases: Coenzyme forms of the B vitamins
concepts.arabicLabel: الفيتامينات الذائبة في الماء ووظائفها كإنزيمات مساعدة
arabicAliases: الأشكال المساعدة للفيتامينات الذائبة في الماء
concepts.definition: Vitamin C and the B complex are water-soluble, absorbed directly into blood, not stored except for folate and B12, and their deficiencies appear quickly. Each has one function a matching question uses. Thiamine, as thiamine pyrophosphate, runs the oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids and transketolase; deficiency is beriberi. Riboflavin, as FMN and FAD, and niacin, as NAD⁺ and NADP⁺, are hydrogen carriers; niacin deficiency is pellagra. Pantothenic acid is the vitamin of coenzyme A and is the acyl carrier. Biotin runs carboxylation, that is, CO₂ fixation. Folic acid, as tetrahydrofolate, transfers one-carbon units; deficiency gives megaloblastic anaemia and neural tube defects. Cobalamin converts homocysteine to methionine and methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, and its deficiency gives subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. Vitamin C is the water-soluble antioxidant, and pyridoxal phosphate sits at each catalytic site of muscle glycogen phosphorylase.
concepts.explicitObjective: Match each water-soluble vitamin to the reaction or the deficiency the book names for it, and identify which options in a matching list belong to a vitamin that is not in the stem.
concepts.pitfalls: Choosing niacin for "oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids" because both involve NAD⁺. The decarboxylation coenzyme is thiamine pyrophosphate; niacin's answer is pellagra. The second reliable loss is pairing folate with the neurological option: folate deficiency gives neural tube defects in the newborn, while subacute combined degeneration of the cord is B12, and treating a megaloblastic anaemia with folate alone is exactly the mistake the book warns about.

concepts.label: Phenylketonuria is deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, and the mousy odour comes from the metabolites phenylalanine is diverted into
concepts.definition: Phenylalanine is an essential amino acid converted to tyrosine by phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), which needs tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as its hydrogen donor. Most cases of phenylketonuria are a deficiency of PAH itself; about 1–2 per cent are a deficiency of BH4. Phenylalanine that cannot become tyrosine is metabolised instead to phenylpyruvate, phenyl-lactate and phenylacetate, and these rise in tissues, plasma and urine. They are what give the urine its characteristic musty, mousy odour.
concepts.explicitObjective: Given an infant with a mousy urine odour and raised phenylpyruvate, name the diagnosis and the deficient enzyme, and say what the raised metabolites are made from.
concepts.pitfalls: Naming tyrosinase as the deficient enzyme because the child is pale. Tyrosinase deficiency is albinism, a different disease in the same chapter; in PKU tyrosinase is present and merely inhibited. The other error is forgetting the BH4 minority, which matters because those 1–2 per cent do not respond to diet alone.

concepts.label: Salvage returns a free purine base to the nucleotide pool in one step, and it is the major route in brain and red cell precursors
concepts.definition: The salvage system rebuilds a purine nucleotide from a base that has already been made, and the book gives its significance as supplying purine nucleotides to tissues where de novo synthesis is not active — naming the brain and the precursors of red blood cells. It has two arms. Free bases are salvaged in a single step by transfer of the ribose phosphate of PRPP: adenine phosphoribosyl transferase makes AMP from adenine, and hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase makes IMP from hypoxanthine and GMP from guanine, releasing pyrophosphate each time. Nucleosides are salvaged separately by adenosine kinase, which phosphorylates adenosine to AMP and deoxyadenosine to dAMP using ATP. Three bases, two transferases, one shared substrate.
concepts.explicitObjective: Name the two tissues that depend on salvage, list the three salvageable free bases with their enzymes and products, and separate the free-base arm from the nucleoside arm by enzyme and phosphate donor.
concepts.pitfalls: Naming only the two bases in HGPRT's own name and forgetting that a second transferase exists for adenine — the commonest way to get "which free purine bases can be salvaged" wrong. The other error is putting adenosine kinase in the free-base arm: a nucleoside already carries its ribose and needs a kinase, while a free base needs a phosphoribosyl transferase and PRPP, which is why the two arms cannot share an enzyme.

uncertainty: The book names the brain and red cell precursors as the salvage-dependent tissues with "e.g.", so the list is illustrative rather than complete, and it gives no measure of how much of each tissue's nucleotide supply salvage actually provides. It also does not say why de novo synthesis is inactive in those tissues.
evidenceGaps: Supported by the department book only. The book carries the salvage reactions as diagrams rather than prose, so the enzyme, substrate and product of each step are read off the schemes
the significance sentence is the only prose statement. No independent verification has been attached.
